title: Selection, Phenotyping, Progeny Testing and Trait Stability

content.overview: Selection is a repeatable evidence process, not simply choosing the most impressive plant. Strong breeding decisions define traits before evaluation, measure them consistently, control or document environmental differences, preserve population context, compare relatives, retain rejected records, and use progeny performance to determine whether an attractive phenotype is actually useful for inheritance.

vocabulary.definition: Systematic measurement or description of observable traits using defined methods.
The degree to which some individuals are favored over others for reproduction.
The difference between the average phenotype of selected individuals and the average of the population from which they were chosen.
Evaluation of descendants to estimate how reliably a selected parent's traits are transmitted.
Repeated evaluation of genotypes, families or conditions to reduce the influence of chance and local environmental effects.
Consistency of trait inheritance or expression across relevant generations and environments.

sections.title: Define the breeding objective before seeing winners
sections.body: Selection criteria should be written before final ranking so breeders do not redefine success around whichever individual happens to be most visually impressive. Traits should include a measurement method, desired direction and any disqualifying conditions.

sections.title: Phenotyping must be repeatable
sections.body: Trait scores become more useful when observers use the same definitions, developmental stage, sampling position and measurement method. Vague labels such as best aroma or strongest plant are difficult to compare across generations unless operational definitions are recorded.

sections.title: Environmental advantage can mimic genetic superiority
sections.body: A plant in a brighter, cooler or less crowded position may outperform genetically related plants for environmental reasons. Randomization, replication or at minimum detailed environmental records reduce the risk of selecting local advantage instead of inherited potential.

sections.title: Selection pressure changes both gain and diversity
sections.body: Very intense selection can concentrate preferred phenotypes quickly but also reduce genetic diversity and increase the chance that useful alternative alleles are lost. The appropriate intensity depends on population size, breeding stage and goals.

sections.title: Record the starting population, not only winners
sections.body: Without records for rejected individuals, breeders cannot reconstruct trait frequencies, selection intensity or whether later progress reflects a genuine population shift. Preserve enough population-level information to understand what was selected from.

sections.title: Correlated traits can move together
sections.body: Selecting strongly for one characteristic can unintentionally change other traits because of genetic correlations, linkage or shared physiology. Track important secondary traits instead of assuming selection acts on one isolated characteristic.

sections.title: Progeny testing estimates transmitting value
sections.body: A selected individual has breeding value when descendants repeatedly receive useful traits or combinations. Comparing progeny from multiple parents under similar conditions is stronger evidence than ranking the parents from appearance alone.

sections.title: Replication separates repeatable performance from one-off expression
sections.body: Repeating related genotypes, clones, families or environments helps reveal whether a trait ranking is robust. A phenotype that disappears under replication should be interpreted more cautiously than one that repeats consistently.

sections.title: Stability claims require defined evidence
sections.body: Stable, uniform and fixed should refer to explicit observations across enough descendants, generations and conditions for the breeding goal. These terms should not be marketing substitutes for one strong selection cycle.

workedExamples: A plant ranks first for vigor but occupied the brightest corner. Before selecting it as a parent, compare environmental records or replicated performance so position is not mistaken for genetic superiority.

A selected parent has exceptional aroma but only a small fraction of its progeny reproduce the trait. The phenotype was attractive, but the progeny test provides weak evidence of reliable transmission.

A breeder keeps only two plants from a large variable population. This creates high selection pressure but also a strong reduction in represented diversity, which should be an intentional tradeoff rather than an unnoticed consequence.

One family has a slightly lower mean score but far greater uniformity across descendants than another family. Depending on the breeding objective, that repeatability may be more valuable than the single highest individual score.
commonMistakes: Changing selection criteria after seeing the population.
Using vague trait labels without repeatable measurement rules.
Ignoring environmental position and developmental stage.
Applying extreme selection pressure without considering population size or diversity.
Calling a parent genetically superior from phenotype alone.
Declaring a line stable after one generation or one environment.
content.practicalApplication: Design a selection worksheet with breeding objective, trait definitions, measurement methods, parentage, generation, population size, environmental notes, individual scores, rejection reasons, selected parents and progeny results. Use a simulated dataset to explain which selections are well supported, which may reflect environmental bias, and what evidence would be needed before claiming stability.
content.summary: Selection turns observations into genetic change only when measurement and mating decisions are disciplined. Predefined traits, consistent phenotyping, environmental context, population records, balanced selection pressure, progeny testing and replication make breeding progress auditable and reduce overconfidence in one exceptional plant.
